### Company description

Fortrea is a global contract research organization that runs phase I to IV clinical trials, clinical pharmacology and consulting for pharmaceutical, biotechnology and medical device customers under full service, functional service provider and hybrid models, in one reporting segment. It was spun out of Labcorp on June 30, 2023 and sold its Enabling Services segment in 2024, so the issuer is a three-year-old entity whose operating history before mid-2023 is carve-out data. Revenue was USD 2,666.7 million over the last twelve months, split about 47% North America, 31% Europe and 21% elsewhere in 2025, and 37.73% of 2025 revenue was pass-through cost that earns no margin.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_ftre-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 5–6; 10-K_2025-12-31_ftre-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 152; calculation C1

The business model supports cash-flow visibility through multi-year contracts, remaining performance obligations of USD 4,390.7 million and backlog of USD 7.3 billion, but most contracts can be ended on 30 to 90 days notice, one customer is 17.2% of revenue and the top twenty are 69%, so visibility is real but conditional. It weakens refinancing confidence because earnings depend on a few customers' research budgets, and it supports liquidity because customers pay in advance, with unearned revenue of USD 525.5 million.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_ftre-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 8; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ftre-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 11; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ftre-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 27
### Ownership and group structure

Fortrea is a public company with dispersed ownership, listed on Nasdaq, and no controlling holder or sponsor is disclosed. Fortrea Holdings Inc. owns Fortrea Inc., the operating subsidiary that conveys receivables to a special purpose entity under the receivables facility; the credit facilities have named obligors including an English borrower, and no guarantor is named in the filings. Structural priority between the notes and the first-lien term loans, and between parent and subsidiary claims, is not established because the legal documents are not supplied.

Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_ftre-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 6; 10-K_2024-12-31_ftre-20241231.htm.jsonl, page 96; 10-K_2025-12-31_ftre-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 188; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ftre-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 11

Governance behaviour is mixed rather than adverse: no dividend, notes repurchased with disposal proceeds and covenant relief paid for with a fee and tighter limits, against an activist agreement, a staggered board until 2028, turnover in the finance role in 2026 and an executive compensation change approved in October 2026. With no sponsor, creditors get no equity cure, so liquidity and operations must carry any stress, and the Medium governance risk level in Business & governance supports monitoring of covenant reporting and capital allocation.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_ftre-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 99; 10-K_2025-12-31_ftre-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 163; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ftre-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 39
### Revenue drivers and pricing power

Revenue follows the conversion of backlog into work, the volume of customers' trials, and pass-through costs that move revenue without moving profit. Revenue was USD 2,842.5 million in 2023, USD 2,696.4 million in 2024 and USD 2,723.4 million in 2025, and nine-month 2026 revenue fell 2.7% to USD 2,006.2 million, but USD 48.3 million of the USD 56.7 million decline was lower pass-through, so revenue excluding it slipped 0.66%. Management attributes the 2026 decline to lower clinical development revenue and weaker demand for functional service provider work, partly offset by clinical pharmacology.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_ftre-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 23; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ftre-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 29; calculation C10

Pricing power is not evidenced. Many contracts are fixed-price or fee-for-service with a cap, which leaves cost overruns with Fortrea, customers can end most contracts on 30 to 90 days notice or internalise functional service provider resources, and management cites price competition as a risk. Revenue is therefore contract-backed but cancellable, concentrated, partly pass-through and cyclical with customers' research budgets, not structurally declining; the implication is that volume loss, not price, is the mechanism that would move earnings and cash first.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_ftre-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 44; 10-K_2025-12-31_ftre-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 50; 10-K_2025-12-31_ftre-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 79
### Cost structure and margin resilience

Costs are mainly people and pass-through: direct costs, including pass-through, were 79.9% of nine-month 2026 revenue against 81.9% a year earlier, and segment selling and administrative costs fell 9.33% as restructuring actions took effect. The filings do not split costs into fixed and variable, but the stated contribution after direct costs of 20.05% of revenue, with selling costs largely fixed, means each USD 100 million of lost revenue removes about USD 20.05 million of EBITDA before any cost response.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_ftre-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 23; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ftre-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 30; calculation C9

Margins can be defended against a modest volume fall because restructuring has already cut selling costs and capital spending is flexible, but not against the loss of a large customer, wage inflation or adverse mix: merit wage increases and higher variable compensation partly offset savings in 2026, and restructuring charges of USD 32.5 million over the last twelve months show the cost base is still being reset. The implication is that margin resilience depends on volume, which is the weakest part of the credit.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_ftre-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 30; 10-K_2025-12-31_ftre-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 105; calculation C2
### Capital intensity and FCF conversion

Capital intensity is low: capital spending was 0.93% of 2025 revenue and 1.26% of nine-month 2026 revenue, so EBITDA converts to cash with little reinvestment, and spending of USD 32.8 million over the last twelve months leaves limited room to cut. Conversion is poor for other reasons: cash interest was USD 77.8 million, cash taxes USD 14.50 million and restructuring cash payments USD 23.6 million in nine months 2026, so free cash flow before working capital is USD 23.5 million, or 25.68% of reported EBITDA and 18.95% of house-adjusted EBITDA.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_ftre-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 4; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ftre-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 12; calculation C5

Working capital swings dominate: USD 145.5 million of inflow lifted last twelve months free cash flow to USD 169.0 million, USD 132.8 million of it in the fourth quarter of 2025, and receivables of USD 300.0 million are sold off the balance sheet while unbilled services are 81.99% of gross receivables, so cash depends on billing milestones and customer advances. The implication for debt service is that free cash flow can repay debt only if working capital does not reverse, and the maturity wall in 2028 arrives before earnings-based free cash flow has had time to build.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_ftre-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 153; calculation C5; calculation C6
### Porter's Five Forces

Rivalry is intense and is the force that most affects margin: the industry is highly fragmented, with hundreds of small providers and a few large full-service ones, consolidation is led by the larger providers, and price competition could reduce revenue and profitability, which matters because segment margin is only 5.42% of nine-month revenue. Buyer power is high and is the second material force: customers are concentrated, most contracts end on 30 to 90 days notice and large pharmaceutical customers seek significant research cost reductions, so cancellations and price pressure transmit directly to revenue and cash flow.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_ftre-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 22; 10-K_2025-12-31_ftre-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 21; 10-K_2025-12-31_ftre-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 50

The other three forces are secondary for credit. Substitutes exist where customers use in-house departments or internalise functional service provider resources; new entrants are not evidenced as a source of pricing pressure in the sources; supplier power sits with clinical sites, investigators and technology vendors and, for labour, with wage inflation, which affects cost but is not quantified. None of these changes the conclusion that rivalry and buyer power determine margin durability.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_ftre-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 15; 10-K_2025-12-31_ftre-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 19; 10-K_2025-12-31_ftre-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 44
### PEST analysis

Two factors are material to credit. Economic conditions matter because customers' research budgets and biotechnology funding set demand: management says biotechnology funding slowed in the first half of 2025 and strengthened in the second half, and forecasts research spending by large biopharmaceutical companies to grow about 4% to 5% a year over 2025 to 2030 while the contract research market grows more slowly in the short term, so demand is cyclical and a funding slowdown would show first in new awards and cancellations. Regulation matters because the industry is subject to extensive rules with penalties for violations, but the company states it is in compliance in all material respects and no regulatory proceeding is disclosed. Social and technological factors, including artificial intelligence investment, do not appear to be a primary credit driver on the evidence supplied.
### SWOT

- Strengths: liquidity of USD 668.3 million before the acquisition's cash payment and only scheduled amortization of up to USD 25.0 million a year before June 30, 2028; cost actions that lifted segment operating income by 101.30% in nine months; contracted backlog of USD 7.3 billion; low capital intensity; and creditor-friendly conduct with no dividend.

- Weaknesses: net leverage of 9.12x on reported EBITDA and 6.73x on a house-adjusted basis; interest cover of 1.18x; a largest customer at 17.2% of revenue; free cash flow of USD 23.5 million before working capital; and no sponsor, rating or price to support refinancing.

- Opportunities: a stable top line would let cost savings reach cash and bring adjusted leverage toward the covenant steps; the early-phase acquisition adds clinical pharmacology capacity in the segment management says is growing; and an extension of the 2028 maturities would remove the main refinancing risk.

- Threats: loss or reduction of work by the largest customer; further backlog adjustments; a reversal of customer advances; the covenant steps to 5.50x and 5.30x; rating-change rights of the receivables agent; and turnover in the finance role during the refinancing window.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C1; calculation C3; calculation C8; calculation C9
### Financial profile and credit quality

On the nine dimensions the profile is weak overall. Scale and market position are average: revenue of USD 2,666.7 million is sizeable, but market share and peers are not supplied. Competitive advantage is weak on the evidence, because the margin fell from 5.97% in 2023 to 3.21% in 2025 and backlog and obligations are shrinking. Business diversification is weak: one segment and a concentrated customer base, with geography the only broad spread. Cost and capex flexibility is average, since capital spending is 1.26% of revenue and selling costs have been cut, but personnel-heavy direct costs follow revenue down slowly. Margin stability is weak, with reported EBITDA negative in 2024 and 2025 and USD 91.5 million over the last twelve months.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C2; calculation C10

Free cash flow stability is weak, because USD 145.5 million of working capital inflow separates free cash flow of USD 169.0 million from USD 23.5 million before it. Ability to refinance is weak: leverage of 9.12x, maturities from June 30, 2028 and no sponsor, rating or price. Liquidity position is average: USD 668.3 million is ample for 12 months but the revolver ends with the term loan A maturity and its use depends on covenants. Financial policy and governance are average: conduct has favoured creditors, but the finance role has turned over and covenant relief was needed. The trend is improving from a low point, the main supports are liquidity, cost actions and contracted revenue, the main constraints are leverage, concentration and the 2028 wall, and the key missing datapoints are the covenant ratio and definition, the issuer's adjusted EBITDA, ratings and market prices.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C1; calculation C5; calculation C7
### Outlook, tailwinds and headwinds

Over the next 12 to 24 months the outcome turns on three observable events: the covenant tests of December 31, 2026 and 2027, which step to 5.50x and 5.30x; the fourth-quarter report, which shows whether backlog and obligations stabilise after the USD 558 million reduction and whether the year-end working capital pattern repeats; and the handling of the 2028 maturities, which enter their final 12 months on June 30, 2027. A tailwind is the continuing effect of restructuring that runs through 2026 and lower interest after the notes repurchase; a headwind is the loss of work from concentrated customers, which management does not quantify.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2024-12-31_ftre-20241231.htm.jsonl, page 96; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ftre-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 28; calculation C7

Over three to five years, management expects research and development spending to grow and outsourcing to remain elevated, but also says the contract research market will grow more slowly in the short term. Sector tailwinds are growing pipelines, complex trials and a recovery in biotechnology funding; sector headwinds are slower growth, price competition and customer consolidation. For credit the implication is that the 2030 maturities of USD 649.0 million fall in a period when sector growth could help earnings, but only if the 2028 refinancing succeeds first and leverage has fallen toward the covenant level.
### Downside scenario

The realistic downside begins with the largest customer halving its work, which the backlog adjustment and the 30 to 90 days termination rights show is possible. On 17.2% of last twelve months revenue, that removes USD 229.34 million of revenue; at the 20.05% contribution rate and with selling costs fixed, contribution falls by USD 45.99 million, taking reported EBITDA to USD 45.51 million and house-adjusted EBITDA to USD 78.01 million. Cover of cash interest falls to 0.58x reported and 1.00x adjusted, house-adjusted net leverage rises to 10.70x, and free cash flow before working capital turns to an outflow of USD 22.49 million a year.
Basis: calculation C9

Liquidity does not break first: cash of USD 220.6 million, before the acquisition's payment that Financial foundation does not carry into pro forma cash, covers the outflow for years, and if unearned revenue fell by 10%, USD 52.55 million, the annual outflow of USD 75.04 million would still be covered for 2.94 years by cash alone. The break comes through leverage and refinancing: covenant tests at 5.50x and 5.30x would be harder to meet, which could block the revolver, and cash of USD 220.6 million is USD 166.90 million short of the USD 387.50 million of term loan A due June 30, 2028, so the business would need a refinancing from a weaker position. Management levers are selling and administrative cost cuts, capital spending of USD 32.8 million, the absence of dividends and the revolver; resilience appears sufficient to avoid liquidity distress through 2027 but not to repay the 2028 maturities without refinancing.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_ftre-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 16; 10-K_2025-12-31_ftre-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 164; calculation C7; calculation C9
### Overall credit view

Overall, Fortrea presents a weak business profile supported by liquidity of USD 668.3 million, cost actions that doubled segment operating income and USD 7.3 billion of backlog, but credit quality is constrained by net leverage of 9.12x reported EBITDA, a largest customer at 17.2% of revenue and free cash flow that depends on working capital. Cash-flow durability appears weak because USD 23.5 million of free cash flow before working capital must carry USD 77.8 million of cash interest through a business whose revenue is cancellable. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on EBITDA recovery toward the covenant steps, extension of the June 30, 2028 maturities and the absence of a rating-change event for the receivables facility.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C1; calculation C5; calculation C7

Primary downside path: loss of work from the largest customer removes contribution that is about equal to reported EBITDA, covenant tests tighten and the 2028 maturities cannot be repaid from cash. Business profile against typical leveraged-credit issuers in the sector is not established because no peer data is supplied. Further analysis would require the covenant ratio and definition, the executed credit documents, the issuer's adjusted EBITDA, ratings and market prices, the proxy statement and the fourth-quarter report. Fundamental credit completed. Top risk: customer concentration feeding into leverage and the 2028 refinancing.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C9
